opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd put it a little more carefully. It's not blind confidence. Simulation is a tool, and like any tool it has strengths and failure modes. But I've come to believe it's an extraordinarily powerful one, especially for robotics.

Think about how a child learns to walk. A toddler falls hundreds of times a day. That's tremendous experience, and the child doesn't break. If you try to get that much experience on a physical robot, you run into practical problems. The robot breaks, you need a person to reset it, and you can only run one robot in real time. In simulation you can run thousands of copies in parallel, faster than real time, and nothing gets damaged. Learning methods like reinforcement learning are very hungry for experience, so simulation is what makes them viable.

The obvious objection is the "sim-to-real gap": the simulator is never a perfect model of the world. Friction is wrong, the motors behave differently, the terrain isn't what you modeled. That's true, and for a long time people concluded that policies trained in simulation wouldn't transfer. But I think the lesson is that you shouldn't try to build a perfect simulator. You should train across a wide variety of simulated conditions, with different masses, frictions, and terrains, and teach the system to adapt online. Then the real world is just one more variation it has to handle. In our work on legged locomotion, that's essentially what happened. The robot learned to estimate, implicitly and in a fraction of a second, what kind of situation it was in and adjust its behavior, much the way you adjust when you step from pavement onto sand.

There's also a broader scientific point. In classical control engineering, you write down a model and derive a controller analytically. That works beautifully when the model is tractable. But contact-rich, messy, real-world interaction quickly becomes intractable to analyze by hand. Simulation lets you keep the physics while handing the hard part, discovering the controller, to learning. You get the best of both: the structure we understand from physics, and the flexibility of learning from experience.

So my confidence comes from results. We've seen behaviors learned entirely in simulation work robustly on real hardware, on stairs, rocks, and slippery surfaces. I don't think simulation replaces real-world experience entirely; ultimately you want robots that keep learning in the world. But as a way to bootstrap competence, I think it's one of the most important developments in the field.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation lets us keep the physics while learning discovers the controller, avoiding the need to analyze messy interactions by hand when they are intractable.

r002.rationale: It describes the simulator as an imperfect model of the world, with modeled friction, motors, and terrain.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the pace of computing improvements with the slower pace of human ingenuity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me first say that I don't place unconditional confidence in simulation. I think of it as one tool, and a very powerful one, but you have to understand where it works and where it doesn't.

Let me start with where I come from. I'm a vision person by background, and in computer vision we spent decades, really, working from data. You collect images, you label them, you train models. And that paradigm has been enormously successful. But when you move to robotics, you run into a very hard problem, which is that collecting data in the physical world is expensive, it's slow, and it can be dangerous. If I want to train a legged robot to walk, I cannot let it fall ten thousand times on a real staircase. The hardware breaks, and more fundamentally, I can't get the millions of trials that modern learning methods want.

So simulation is, in some sense, forced on us. If you believe that learning from large amounts of experience is the way to get robust behavior, which I do, then you need a place where that experience is cheap. And in simulation, time is essentially free. You can run thousands of copies of the robot in parallel, you can randomize the terrain, the friction, the mass of the limbs, and you can get years of experience in a few hours of compute.

Now, the obvious objection is the sim-to-real gap. The simulator is never a perfect model of the world. And this is true. But what we've learned, and this came out very clearly in the legged locomotion work, is that you don't need the simulator to be exactly right. You need it to be right in distribution. If you train a policy across a wide enough range of physical parameters, the real world ends up being just one more sample from that distribution, and the policy adapts. So the trick is not to build a perfect simulator. The trick is to build a diverse one, and to put the burden on the learning algorithm to cope with the variation.

There's also a deeper point about science here. Historically, in physics, in engineering, we understood systems by writing down equations and analyzing them. But for the kinds of systems we care about in robotics, contact-rich dynamics, deformable objects, a robot hand manipulating a cube, the equations exist but they're not analytically tractable. Simulation is how we actually explore the consequences of those equations. It plays the role that experiment plays in the natural sciences, except we control everything, which means we can do the kind of controlled, repeatable study that is very hard to do with physical hardware.

Where I'm more cautious is perception. Simulating the visual world, the appearance of objects, lighting, textures, that's much harder than simulating rigid-body physics, and I think that's where real-world data still matters enormously. So my view is actually a hybrid one. Learn the control, the motor skills, in simulation, where physics is well understood and cheap to compute. Learn the perception from real data, where the world is the only faithful source. And find clean interfaces between the two.

So the confidence isn't that simulation is the truth. It's that simulation is where we can afford to fail, and failure, lots of it, is how these systems learn.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation helps explore systems whose equations are not analytically tractable, but does not state that simulation avoids simplifying assumptions previously needed for tractable mathematical analysis.

r002.rationale: It describes simulation as modeling the world and exploring consequences of physical equations, with variation in physical parameters such as friction and mass.

r003.rationale: The response discusses cheap, parallel simulation, but does not compare computing power improving rapidly with human ingenuity improving more slowly.

astra-6.text:
Well, simulation lets us explore the consequences of a model in situations where we cannot work them out analytically. You can have relatively simple physical laws, but once many things interact, the resulting behavior becomes very complicated. A computer gives us a way to follow those interactions and ask, “If I change this, what happens?”

For control engineering, that is particularly useful because you can test a controller repeatedly, including under conditions that would be expensive or dangerous to create in the real world. You can vary the conditions, examine failures, and improve the design.

But the confidence has to be qualified. A simulation tells you what follows from your model; it does not establish that your model is correct. You still need experiments and comparisons with reality. So I see simulation as part of a loop: build a model, make predictions, test them, and revise the model. Its power comes from that connection to experiment.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says simulation shows what follows from a model and describes building a model before making predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would distinguish between confidence in simulation as a tool and confidence in a particular simulator. A simulator is only as good as the assumptions that go into it. But it gives us something extremely valuable: we can conduct experiments cheaply, repeatedly, and under controlled conditions. We can change one thing at a time and see what happens.

For control engineering, that means we can explore policies, including policies that would be dangerous to try on a real machine. We can vary the physical parameters and ask whether a controller works only under ideal conditions or across a range of conditions.

Of course, the ultimate test is the real world. You have to compare the predictions of the simulation with measurements and understand where they disagree. So my confidence is in that process: build a model, experiment with it, test it against reality, and improve it. Simulation makes that cycle much more powerful.
